newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy has epic battle on its hands to make EMU.
newsitem.headline: Italy has epic battle on its hands to make EMU.

text.p: Italy's uphill struggle to take the lira back into Europe's Exchange Rate Mechanism (ERM) is only a foretaste of the battle it faces over the next two years to whip itself into shape for currency union.
"The stretch of road leading to a single currency is now short, but it runs tortuous and narrow along the edge of a ravine," Turin's daily newspaper La Stampa said.
Italy parleyed its way back into the EU's currency grid on Sunday, four years after making an embarrasing exit, but had to settle for a significantly stronger rate than it wanted.
After lengthy weekend negotiations EU Finance Ministers and central bankers agreed to let the lira back into the ERM at a central parity rate against the mark of 990 lire.

Prime Minister Romano Prodi, who made no secret he preferred a rate no stonger than 1,000 lire, put a brave face on the outcome, saying it was a big step forward in Italy's campaign to become a founder member of a single currency in 1999.

Italian industrialists were less sanguine. "We are worried by the 990 lire parity level, we will have to measure up to this new exchange rate" said Giorgio Fossa, president of the Italian employers association, Confindustria.
The toughest resistence to Italy's bid for a weaker parity rate came not from France, as had been widely expected, but from the formidable head of Germany's Bundesbank, Hans Tietmeyer.
Prodi said on Monday that France had been the only country at the talks to stand by Italy's call for a 1,000 lire central parity.
"The French were our only strong loyal defenders," Prodi told a business conference in the northeast city of Udine.
Tietmeyer left nobody in any doubt that Italy still has to prove itself if it wants to qualify for European economic and monetary union (EMU) by 1999.
"This is not a prejudicial decision. It is certainly not a comment on Italy's qualification for monetary union," the powerful German central bank chief said after the talks in Brussels.
Economists agreed, saying that despite the lira's return to the ERM, Italy still had its work cut out to meet the tough economic requirements for EMU.
"From an economic point of view rejoining ERM does not make much difference," said Jose Luis Alzola, an economist at Salomon Brothers in London.

Italy's hardest task will be to wrestle down its public sector deficit to within three percent of gross domestic product (GDP) by the end of 1997 -- one of the key criteria set out in the 1991 Maastricht Treaty that traced out the road to EMU.
The European Union will decide in early 1998 which of the bloc's 15 member nations will be allowed into the magic circle of countries forming a single currency the following year.
That decision will be based on a snapshot of each country's public finances in 1997.

The Italian government has won approval from the lower house of parliament for one of the most stringent budgets in recent years -- a 62.5 trillion lire ($41.61 billion) package of deficit-cutting measures, including a controversial income tax supplement.
Italy is set to overshoot its deficit target for this year by a wide margin and some economists are forecasting a deficit next year of at least four percent of GDP on present trends.
Government efforts to narrow the gap, a legacy of years of fiscal profligacy, have not been made easier by a sharp economic slowdown which has sliced into tax receipts.
Hopes are pinned on a rapid fall in interest rates bringing a windfall in the form of lower costs for servicing the country's debt mountain -- the main component of the deficit.
But the stronger-than-expected rate for the lira in the ERM could put a brake on interest rate declines.
"Adopting a relatively strong central parity rate makes it harder for the Bank of Italy to cut interest rates unless the lira strengthens significantly," said Alzola. ($1=1502 Lire)
